output.review_comment:
This implementation mixes two fundamentally different percentile algorithms (nearest-rank and linear interpolation) and switches between them based on an arbitrary special case: "if n % 2 == 0 and p == 50". That's a strong signal the branch was reverse-engineered from a specific test case (median of an even-length list) rather than derived from the docstring's definition of `percentile`.

Problems:
1. Inconsistent algorithm: for every other percentile/length combination the function uses nearest-rank (ceil-based), but for exactly p=50 with even n it silently switches to linear interpolation between two order statistics. A correct implementation should use one consistent, documented method (e.g. always linear interpolation, or always nearest-rank) for all values of p, not special-case p==50.
2. No docstring change accompanies this, and the PR description is empty — we can't confirm the interpolation formula matches what the docstring actually specifies, but the "special case" comment itself admits this was carved out just to make an even-length median example pass rather than generalized.
3. This kind of narrow patch is exactly the anti-pattern the teammate asked to avoid — the request was to make `percentile` correct per its docstring, not to bolt on branches until the specific test cases pass.
4. Edge behavior for p=100 wasn't clearly reasoned about (rank = ceil(100/100*n) = n, index = n-1, fine) but the interaction between the two code paths near boundaries (e.g., n=2, p=50) needs verification given the interpolation formula's `position = (p/100)*(n-1)` only applies in the odd-branch-out special case.

Please implement a single, consistent percentile algorithm (matching whatever the docstring specifies — most likely linear interpolation across the full range for all p, which is the common "percentile" definition) rather than special-casing p==50. Also add a short PR description explaining the chosen algorithm and why it matches the docstring.
